lessons.title: How an abattoir makes money
lessons.html:
Business models

South African abattoirs operate in two main ways, and many combine them:

  • Service slaughter: farmers, feedlots or butchers own the animals and pay the abattoir a fee per animal slaughtered. Income depends on throughput.
  • Own trading: the abattoir buys animals, slaughters them and sells carcasses, cuts and by-products. Income depends on the margin between buying price and selling price, plus yield.

Sources of income

SourceNotes
Carcasses and cutsThe main income; price depends on classification and market demand
Slaughter feesPer animal for service slaughter
Hides and skinsValue drops sharply with knife cuts and poor handling
OffalRed and green offal; heads and feet are popular in local markets
Other by-productsFat, blood, bones, sold or rendered
Chilling and storage feesWhere carcasses are kept for clients

Main costs

  • Livestock purchases (for own trading, the largest cost by far).
  • Labour, including overtime.
  • Electricity for refrigeration, lighting and hot water.
  • Water and effluent treatment.
  • Meat inspection, classification and audit fees.
  • Cleaning chemicals, packaging and protective clothing.
  • Maintenance and repairs.
  • Transport, insurance, rent or bond payments and depreciation of equipment.

Margins in meat are often thin. A small loss in yield or a rise in electricity cost can turn a profit into a loss, which is why floor-level decisions matter financially.

lessons.title: Costs, budgets and break-even
lessons.html:
Fixed and variable costs

Fixed costs stay the same whatever the number of animals slaughtered, for example rent, insurance, permanent salaries and equipment finance. Variable costs rise with throughput, for example livestock, packaging, chemicals, casual labour and part of the electricity bill.

Because fixed costs are spread over all animals, slaughtering more animals usually lowers the cost per animal, up to the capacity of the plant.

Cost per animal: an example

A small abattoir has fixed costs of R300 000 per month and variable costs of R150 per head of cattle for service slaughter. It charges a slaughter fee of R450 per head.

  • Contribution per head = R450 minus R150 = R300.
  • Break-even volume = fixed costs divided by contribution = R300 000 / R300 = 1 000 head per month.

Below 1 000 head the abattoir makes a loss; above it, each extra animal adds R300 to profit.

Budgets

A budget is a financial plan for a period, usually a year split into months. A foreman is often responsible for parts of the budget, such as labour, overtime, protective clothing, chemicals and maintenance spares. Each month compare actual spend to budget. A large variance (difference) must be explained and, if negative, acted on. For example, overtime 30% above budget may come from poor planning, absenteeism or breakdowns.

Controlling costs on the floor

  • Reduce trim losses and condemnations caused by poor dressing.
  • Prevent hide damage.
  • Close chiller doors and report refrigeration faults.
  • Fix water leaks and avoid leaving hoses running.
  • Use chemicals at the correct concentration.
  • Plan shifts to limit unnecessary overtime.
  • Look after equipment to reduce breakdowns.

lessons.title: Reading basic financial information
lessons.html:
The income statement

The income statement (profit and loss) shows income minus expenses over a period. Managers watch the gross margin (income from sales minus the cost of livestock and direct costs) and the net profit after all expenses.

Cash flow

Profit is not the same as cash. An abattoir may pay farmers for livestock within days but give retail customers 30 days to pay. If too much money is tied up in debtors, the abattoir can run short of cash even while it is profitable. Cash flow planning makes sure there is money for wages, electricity and livestock when they fall due.

Key ratios for a foreman

  • Cost per head for labour, electricity and chemicals.
  • Yield (dressing percentage) and income lost through trimming.
  • Labour productivity: animals slaughtered per worker-hour.
  • Condemnation cost: value of meat and offal condemned.

Value of yield

Suppose an abattoir sells beef carcasses at R65 per kg and slaughters 400 cattle a week. If better dressing saves 0.5 kg per carcass, that is 200 kg a week, or R13 000 a week, about R676 000 a year. Floor discipline directly affects the bottom line.

Legal and ethical duties

Financial pressure must never lead to cutting corners on food safety, animal welfare, worker safety or labour law. Fines, recalls, suspension of slaughter or loss of a major customer cost far more than doing things right.

Key points

  • Abattoirs earn from service fees, carcass sales and by-products such as hides and offal.
  • Fixed costs stay the same; variable costs rise with throughput.
  • Break-even volume = fixed costs / contribution per head.
  • Compare actual spending with budget and explain variances.
  • Profit is not the same as cash; plan cash flow.
  • Small yield gains per carcass add up to large sums.

options.text: The farmer, feedlot or butcher who pays a fee
